Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the first page of an onboarding document for a new backend engineer joining a payments team. Around 200 words.

Welcome to the payments team. You're joining the group that moves money for the company — every charge, refund, and payout runs through services we own. Correctness here has a different cost than most backend work: a bug can mean a customer charged twice, a merchant paid late, or a reconciliation report that doesn't add up at month end.

Your first two weeks focus on three things. First, read the ledger service code and its tests — it's the source of truth for every balance in the system, and understanding how it enforces double-entry accounting will make the rest of the codebase click. Second, sit in on an on-call handoff, even though you won't carry the pager yet. You'll hear how incidents actually get diagnosed, which teaches you more about the system than any doc. Third, ship one small fix to a low-risk service in your first week — we'll pick something in the reporting pipeline, not the charge path.

A few things that make this team different: every write to the ledger is idempotent, keyed by a request ID the caller supplies. We never delete a payment record; we reverse it with a new entry. And every PR touching money movement needs two reviewers, one of them from the payments-core group.

Your manager will walk you through account setup and access requests tomorrow.

Add a section on who to ask for what.

Who to ask

For questions about ledger schema or double-entry rules, ask the payments-core team in #payments-core. For payout timing and merchant-facing issues, ask the payouts team — they own the batching schedule and the bank file format. For anything touching PCI scope or card data handling, ask security before you write code, not after.

Access requests for the ledger database and the reconciliation dashboard go through your manager, not IT. Production incidents outside business hours page whoever is on call; check the PagerDuty schedule rather than messaging a specific person. For code review on anything touching money movement, tag payments-core in the PR — the on-call handoff will tell you who's active that week.
